chapters.title: Some greeks add and some only look like they do
chapters.dek: Addition is a statement about units. Get the units right and the aggregation question answers itself.

figures.title: Every position's contribution, and what survives netting
figures.caption: Switch the measure and watch the netting change character. Dollar delta nets to something modest out of large opposing legs; gamma cash nets to almost nothing out of two legs twenty times its size. The ratio of the net to the gross is the single best one-glance indicator of how much a summary number is hiding.

checks.q: A book shows gamma cash of $2,000 per 1%, assembled from a −$18,000 leg and a +$20,000 leg. What should worry you?
checks.right: That the net only holds at today's spot. Two large opposing gamma positions at different strikes stop offsetting as soon as spot moves, so the small net is a statement about a moment
checks.why: The offset is local. Each leg's gamma is a hill centered on its own strike — the same fact that made page 11's log contract necessary — so a book flat by netting at 102 can be substantially long or short gamma at 95 or 115. This is exactly why chapter 02 exists: a single netted number describes one point, and a matrix describes the neighborhood.

chapters.text: The first thing that goes wrong when you put positions together is that people add numbers which are not in the same units. A delta of 0.54 on one option and 0.31 on another do not sum to anything meaningful, because delta is a rate — shares per share — and the two options are written on different quantities of stock. Convert to money first and the problem disappears. Dollar delta adds , on one underlying, without qualification. Multiply delta by the contract multiplier, by the position size, and by spot, and you have a number of dollars that moves one-for-one with a percentage change in the stock. Our four-position book carries a share delta of 557 — about $57,000 of exposure — assembled from legs of −2,496, +1,430, +709 and +914 shares. Gamma cash adds , once expressed as dollars of delta gained per 1% move. Our book's is $2,042 per percent, and it is worth noticing how it got there: the short front-month 100 calls contribute −$18,002 and the long 110 calls +$20,033 . Two large opposing numbers netting to something small is the normal condition of an options book, and it is precisely the condition under which a net figure stops describing the risk. Vega adds arithmetically and lies. You can total it — ours is $417 per volatility point — but the total presumes every volatility moves together, which is the one thing volatilities reliably do not do. Chapter 04 takes this apart. And two things do not add at all. Gamma across different underlyings is not additive in any useful sense, because a 1% move in one name is not the same event as a 1% move in another; you need a covariance structure, which is page 12's subject. Greeks across dates are not comparable either — a one-week gamma and a one-year gamma are different animals wearing the same label. [equation: $Δ = Δ × multiplier × contracts × S Γ_cash = Γ × multiplier × contracts × S² × 1%] Reads as: turn every rate into money before you add anything up. The conversion is mechanical and skipping it is the most common error on a real blotter. chapters.title: The grid a risk manager actually reads
chapters.dek: Reprice the whole book in every cell. Then put the greek prediction beside it and look at the difference.

figures.title: Spot across, volatility down — the whole book, repriced
figures.caption: Flip between the three views on the same grid. Full reprice and greek estimate look broadly similar in the middle four cells and diverge everywhere else; the error view makes the pattern obvious in one glance. Notice that the largest error is not in the worst cell — the greeks fail hardest where the book is making money, which is why "the model was conservative" is not a defense.

checks.q: Your greek report and your scenario matrix disagree about a −20% cell by $12,000. Which is wrong?
checks.right: Neither. The matrix is the book's actual value there; the greek report is a local expansion around today's spot and was never meant to be accurate 20% away
checks.why: Neither is wrong; they answer different questions. Greeks are derivatives evaluated at a point and their accuracy decays with distance from that point — chapter 03 measures how fast. Treating a disagreement as a reconciliation break rather than as expected behavior is a common and expensive misunderstanding, because the fix people reach for is to "correct" the matrix.

terms.Scenario matrix: A grid of full repricings across spot and volatility. Unlike a greek report it does not degrade with distance from today's spot, which is why limits are set on it.

chapters.text: A greek report is a description of the book at one point, expressed in derivatives. A scenario matrix is the book itself, evaluated at many points. The difference between them is the subject of this page, and the fastest way to see it is to compute both and subtract. The grid below moves spot across the columns and volatility down the rows and puts the full repriced P&L in each cell. Every position is revalued from scratch at the new spot and the new volatility — no approximations, no local expansions. This is what the book would actually be worth. Then switch the display to error and you are looking at what a greek report would have missed. At the center the errors are trivially small, which is exactly what "the greeks are a local approximation" means. Move to the corners and they are enormous: at spot +20% with volatility up 10 points, the book makes $49,061 and the greek estimate is short by $29,456 — the report would have predicted well under half the move. The asymmetry matters as much as the size. The errors are not symmetric in spot, because gamma is not constant, and they are not symmetric in volatility, because vega is not constant either. A book that looks balanced in the greeks can be strongly convex in one direction and concave in the other, and only the matrix shows it. This is why the matrix, not the greek line, is the artefact that gets escalated. A greek report answers "what is the book doing right now"; a matrix answers "what happens if", and the second question is the one a risk committee is actually asking. chapters.title: How far can you trust a greek report?
chapters.dek: About one percent. After that the answer degrades quickly and in a measurable way.

figures.title: Full reprice against the greek estimate, as the move grows
figures.caption: The lower panel is the one to remember. It is flat and near zero out to a couple of percent and then climbs steeply — there is a knee, and knowing roughly where your book's knee sits is what tells you when to stop quoting greeks and start running scenarios.

checks.q: Adding a third-order term to the estimate would help most in which situation?
checks.right: Large moves, where it is the first missing term and the error grows roughly with the cube of the move
checks.why: Large moves. At small moves the error is already negligible so there is nothing to fix. The reason desks generally do not bother adding higher-order terms is that once you are far enough out for them to matter, a full reprice is both exact and cheap — the approximation exists to save computation that is no longer worth saving.

terms.Attribution: Explaining yesterday's P&L with yesterday's greeks. The residual is a test of your marks and your model, and it is the first thing to read on a risk report.

chapters.text: "The greeks are a local approximation" is true and useless without a number attached. Here is the number. Take our book, move spot, and compare the full reprice against what delta and gamma predicted. At 1% the book makes $582 and the greeks predict $578 — an error of 0.7% , entirely negligible. At 2% the error is 2.7% . At 5% it is 13.8% : the book makes $3,589 and the estimate says $3,093. At 10% the estimate captures barely two-thirds. At 20% the book makes $36,971 and the greeks predict $15,436 — an error of 58% , which is to say the report is wrong by more than it is right. The shape of that decay is the useful part. The dollar error grows roughly like the cube of the move, because delta and gamma capture the first two terms of the expansion and the first thing they miss is the third — so the error as a share of the move , the percentages above, grows roughly like the square. Halve the move and the dollar error falls by about eight; double it and the percentage error roughly quadruples. That is a fast enough exponent that the boundary between "greeks are fine" and "greeks are useless" is narrow, and it sits at a smaller move than most people assume. The practical rule that falls out: use greeks for hedging decisions and daily attribution , where moves are small and the derivative is exactly what you want. Use the matrix for limits, stress and anything that gets escalated, where the moves are large by construction. Using a greek report to answer a stress question is the specific error, and on a book like this one, which is long convexity, it errs in the direction of comfort — it under-predicts big moves in both directions. Do not generalize the sign: on a short straddle the delta-gamma estimate overstates the loss on a big move, because the real gamma fades as spot leaves the strike. The size of the error is universal; its direction belongs to the book. Full reprice against the greek estimate, as the move grows Error as a share of the move The move The lower panel is the one to remember. It is flat and near zero out to a couple of percent and then climbs steeply — there is a knee, and knowing roughly where your book's knee sits is what tells you when to stop quoting greeks and start running scenarios. Derivation — why the error grows like the cube of the move A greek report is the first two terms of a Taylor expansion of the book's value in spot. [equation: V(S+h) = V(S) + Δh + ½Γh² + ⅙·(∂³V/∂S³)·h³ + …] Reads as: value, plus delta times the move, plus half gamma times the move squared, plus a third-order term nobody reports. Delta and gamma are the first two; everything after is what the report is missing. So the error of a delta-plus-gamma estimate is the first term you dropped, and that term carries h³ . [equation: error ≈ ⅙ · speed · h³] Reads as: the mistake grows with the cube of how far the market moved. The third derivative of value with respect to spot is sometimes called speed, and it is largest where gamma is changing fastest — near the strikes. A cubic law is steep. Doubling the move multiplies the error by roughly eight, so the transition from "the greeks are fine" to "the greeks are useless" happens over a surprisingly narrow band of move sizes. Our book's measured percentage errors — 0.7% at 1%, 2.7% at 2%, 13.8% at 5%, 58.2% at 20% — grow roughly like the square of the move, which is the cube law divided by the move itself; the dollar errors, $4 at 1% and $496 at 5%, are the cube law directly. Past about 10% the growth slows, because the higher-order terms that take over do not keep compounding at the same rate. That also explains the shape of the lower panel: it is flat and negligible out to a couple of percent and then turns upward sharply, because a cubic sitting under a linear-plus-quadratic term contributes essentially nothing until it suddenly contributes everything. Where it breaks. The expansion assumes the book's value is smooth in spot, and it is not. A digital or barrier payoff has a discontinuity in value or in delta, at which point no number of Taylor terms converges and the only honest answer is a full reprice — which is the practical argument for building the matrix out of repricings rather than out of higher-order greeks. The expansion also says nothing about paths: two scenarios that end at the same spot with the same volatility can imply very different hedging costs on the way, and a static matrix cell prices neither.

chapters.title: One vega number across the term structure is a lie
chapters.dek: Our book's net vega is 417. Four different volatility moves that all "look like two points" produce P&L from 743 to 1,238.

figures.title: Vega by tenor bucket, and the net that hides it
figures.caption: Drag the front and back shifts independently and watch the actual P&L bar separate from the net-vega prediction. Any point on the line where the two agree is a coincidence of that particular twist, not a property of the book — and the further the surface move is from parallel, the less the single number means.

checks.q: A desk reports net vega of zero. What have you learned?
checks.right: Almost nothing. It could genuinely be flat, or it could be long a thousand in the front against short a thousand in the back — a large term-structure position that nets to zero
checks.why: Almost nothing. The third answer is closest to being right and still misses the point: "hedged against a parallel shift" describes the one scenario that essentially never happens cleanly. This is why bucketed limits exist, and why a risk manager's first question on seeing a zero is not "good" but "show me the buckets".

chapters.text: Vega is quoted as a single figure and it is the most misleading number on a risk report, because summing it presumes that every implied volatility on the surface moves together. They do not. Front-month volatility is jumpy and event-driven; back-month volatility is stable and mean-reverting; and the front can rise five points on an earnings date while the back does not move at all. Our book's vega breaks into +99 in the front two months, −495 in the two-to-six month bucket, and +813 beyond six months, netting to +417 . That net is a true arithmetic total and it describes almost nothing, because the book is really a term-structure position — short the belly, long the wings of the calendar — wearing the disguise of a modest long-vol book. Watch what that does. A genuine parallel move of +2 volatility points makes $863 , close to the naive net-vega prediction of $834. But a front-up-ten, back-down-one-and-a-half twist makes $864 ; a front-down-six, back-up-five twist makes $1,238 ; and a front-up-twelve, back-down-three twist makes $743 . Same book, same net vega, and a spread of nearly 67% between the outcomes — with nothing that a single number could have distinguished. Which is why real risk systems bucket. The convention is a set of tenor buckets with vega reported in each, and the discipline is that limits are set per bucket rather than on the total. A desk that is flat on net vega and running plus-and-minus a thousand in adjacent buckets is not flat; it has a term-structure position that nobody has approved. The same argument applies twice more, and for the same reason. Bucket by strike as well as by tenor, because a book long wings and short the body has zero net vega and a large skew position. And remember from page 07 that the delta you are bucketing is itself model-dependent — sticky-strike and sticky-delta conventions produce different vega attributions from identical prices. Bucketing shows where the vega is. It does not say how to add the buckets, and the answer depends on how much each tenor moves when the front does: page 21, chapter 03 . Vega by tenor bucket, and the net that hides it Four volatility moves, one net vega The volatility move Drag the front and back shifts independently and watch the actual P&L bar separate from the net-vega prediction. Any point on the line where the two agree is a coincidence of that particular twist, not a property of the book — and the further the surface move is from parallel, the less the single number means. Try this Set the front shift to +10 and the back to −1.5. Then flip to front −6, back +5. Predict whether the P&L changes sign, before you look.

chapters.title: Gamma across names needs a common move
chapters.dek: Chapter 01 said gamma does not add across underlyings. It can be made to, once you say what move you are adding it against.

figures.title: P&L of the two-name book when the index moves
figures.caption: The grey curve smiles and the blue one frowns. The sum had the wrong sign because it gave a 1% move in the utility the same weight as a 1% move in a stock that travels four times as far.

checks.q: You are long $200,000 of gamma cash per 1% in a beta-1.5 name and want to offset its index exposure with short SPY gamma. How much SPY gamma cash do you sell?
checks.why: $450,000. 200,000 × 1.5². The $300,000 answer scales by beta once, which is right for delta and wrong for gamma. What you are left with afterwards is the name's own movement around the index, which is the part you presumably wanted.

chapters.text: Two positions. Long gamma worth $1,000,000 of delta per 1% in a utility, and short gamma worth $500,000 per 1% in a technology stock. Add them and the book is long $500,000 per 1%, which says a market move in either direction makes money. The figure moves the index and lets each name follow it by its own beta. P&L of the two-name book when the index moves The two names The grey curve smiles and the blue one frowns. The sum had the wrong sign because it gave a 1% move in the utility the same weight as a 1% move in a stock that travels four times as far. On a 2% index move the summed gamma predicts a gain of $10,000. With the utility at a beta of 0.5 and the technology name at 2.0, the utility moves 1% and makes $5,000 while the technology name moves 4% and loses $40,000. The book loses $35,000. [equation: index-equivalent gamma = Σ Γ_cash × β²] Reads as: before adding, multiply each name's gamma cash by its beta squared. Squared, because beta scales the move and gamma P&L goes with the move squared. Here 1,000,000 × 0.25 − 500,000 × 4 = −$1,750,000 per 1% of index. That number answers one question: what happens when the market moves and everything follows it. It is silent on the days a name moves alone, and for those the original gammas are the right ones, name by name. A book can be short index-equivalent gamma and still make money most days from single-stock noise, which is a dispersion position whether or not anyone called it one. Page 12 is that trade taken on purpose. Beta is an assumption. It is estimated from history, it drifts, and in a selloff betas of defensive names tend to rise toward one, which makes the frown here an understatement of the bad case rather than an overstatement. Try this Predict the beta on the technology name at which the book is flat to an index move, with the utility left at 0.5.

chapters.title: Limits, and the question underneath them
chapters.dek: A limit is not a prediction. It is a statement about how much of a specific bad day the firm is willing to own.

figures.title: Greek limits against the scenario limit
figures.caption: Scale the book up and watch which bar turns first. Every bar grows in proportion — scaling a book scales every repricing too — so what differs is where each one starts. The scenario bar starts higher relative to its limit than the greek bars do, because the scenario loss contains the convexity the greeks are missing, and so it breaches first while every greek is still green. That gap in starting level is the entire argument for having both kinds of limit.

figures.title: Get the book inside its limits
figures.caption: The tempting first move, selling 90-day straddles to fix the back vega, takes three lots and makes gamma worse: with the stock sold to fix delta, gamma falls from −$300,000 to −$460,000 per 1% move, because the straddles you sold were long gamma too. The fix is to buy gamma where it is cheap in vega, at the front. The cheapest book inside every limit sells 18,000 shares, buys four lots of 30-day straddles and sells three of 90-day, for $7,180 of spread.

checks.q: A book is inside every greek limit but breaches its worst-case scenario limit. What is the most likely explanation?
checks.right: The book is convex. Greeks measure the neighborhood of today's spot; the scenario limit is set by a corner where higher-order terms dominate, and chapter 03 showed those reach 58% of the move at 20%
checks.why: The book is convex, and that is what the two limits are for. They are not redundant controls that should agree — they are deliberately different instruments measuring different regions, and the whole reason for running both is that a book can pass one and fail the other. If they always agreed, one of them would be pointless.

terms.Bucketed: Grouped by expiry (or by strike) rather than summed into one number. A net vega of zero across buckets of +1,000 and −1,000 is a term-structure position nobody approved.

chapters.text: Limits look like bureaucracy from a trading seat and like arithmetic from a risk seat, and both readings miss what they are for. A limit is a pre-committed answer to a question nobody can think clearly about while it is happening: how much are we prepared to lose in a scenario we have decided is plausible? They come in layers, and the layers exist because each one fails differently. Greek limits — maximum dollar delta, gamma cash, bucketed vega. Cheap to compute, easy to monitor continuously, and subject to exactly the failure of chapter 03: they describe the book near today's spot and say nothing about the corners. A book can sit inside every greek limit and still be carrying a scenario loss nobody has authorised. Scenario limits — the worst cell of the matrix must be better than some number. This is the one that actually binds, because it is computed from full repricings and therefore does not degrade with move size. Its weakness is that it only covers the scenarios in the grid. Stress limits — named historical or hypothetical events, deliberately chosen because they hurt rather than because they are likely, and usually including a correlation-goes-to-one case for the reasons on page 12 . The figure makes the first layer's weakness concrete. Adjust the position sizes until every greek sits inside its limit, then look at the worst cell of the matrix. It is entirely possible — and on this book, easy — to be green on every greek and red on the scenario, because the greeks are measuring the middle of the grid and the limit that matters lives in a corner. One more thing worth saying plainly, because it is where limits are most often misunderstood. A limit breach is not a prediction that you will lose the money. It is a statement that the position has grown past the size at which the firm is willing to find out. The correct response is to reduce, not to argue about the probability. Greek limits against the scenario limit Utilisation Scale the book up and watch which bar turns first. Every bar grows in proportion — scaling a book scales every repricing too — so what differs is where each one starts. The scenario bar starts higher relative to its limit than the greek bars do, because the scenario loss contains the convexity the greeks are missing, and so it breaches first while every greek is still green. That gap in starting level is the entire argument for having both kinds of limit. Now sit in the morning meeting with a book that is over its limits on all four lines: too long delta, too short gamma, short front vega and long back vega. You have four hedges, each with a bid-offer to pay. Get every line inside its limit and spend as little as you can doing it. The catch is the whole lesson: every hedge moves more than one line. Get the book inside its limits Trade lots The tempting first move, selling 90-day straddles to fix the back vega, takes three lots and makes gamma worse: with the stock sold to fix delta, gamma falls from −$300,000 to −$460,000 per 1% move, because the straddles you sold were long gamma too. The fix is to buy gamma where it is cheap in vega, at the front. The cheapest book inside every limit sells 18,000 shares, buys four lots of 30-day straddles and sells three of 90-day, for $7,180 of spread. Trader's lens A risk manager does not hedge greeks one at a time; every instrument is a vector of greeks, and the job is to find the cheapest combination that lands inside every limit. Traders who hedge line by line overpay, and often fix one breach by creating another. Front options are the cheap source of gamma; back options are the cheap source of vega. Fix delta last, with stock or futures: it is the cheapest greek to move and every option trade changes it. A limit that keeps breaching is telling you the book's real position, not asking for a hedge. Rule of thumb: hedge the greek that is most expensive to move first, and the cheapest one last.

chapters.title: Reading the report end to end
chapters.dek: The order in which you look at it is most of the skill.

figures.title: Daily risk summary
figures.caption: Every line here has appeared in this series with its own chapter. The report is not new information; it is the same information arranged so that a person with four minutes can find the thing that matters.

checks.q: What should you look at first on a daily risk report?
checks.right: Yesterday's P&L against what the greeks predicted. An unexplained residual means the marks or the model are wrong, and every other number on the page inherits that error
checks.why: Attribution first. Every forward-looking number on the report is computed from the same marks and the same model that produced yesterday's prediction. If that prediction failed, the rest of the page is being computed with a broken instrument — and finding that out before you act on the risk numbers is the whole reason attribution is run daily rather than monthly.

chapters.text: Everything above assembles into one page of output that a desk looks at every morning. Reading it well is a routine, and the routine is worth stating explicitly because the natural reading order is close to the worst one. Start with yesterday's P&L against yesterday's prediction. Attribution before position. If the book made money the greeks cannot explain, something is wrong with your marks or your understanding, and no amount of looking at today's risk will surface it. An unexplained residual is the single most informative number on the report. Then the scenario matrix, corners first. Not the greeks. The corners are where the limits bind and where chapter 03 says your intuition is least reliable. Look for asymmetry: a book that loses twice as much down as up is a different animal from one that is symmetric, whatever its delta says. Then bucketed vega and bucketed gamma. Look for large opposing buckets, which chapter 04 showed are invisible in the totals. The question is not "what is the net" but "what is the gross, and is it deliberate". Then the greeks, as a hedging instruction. This is what they are good at: telling you what to trade today. It is the last thing to look at, not the first. Then concentration. How much of the risk is in one name, one expiry, one strike. A book can be well-behaved on every aggregate measure and be a single position with a hedge around it. The table below assembles the report for our four-position book, and the small print underneath it is the part worth internalising: every number in it is conditional on the marks, and the marks on the illiquid lines are somebody's model. A risk report is a measurement of a book made with instruments that the book itself can bend. Daily risk summary Every line here has appeared in this series with its own chapter. The report is not new information; it is the same information arranged so that a person with four minutes can find the thing that matters.

chapters.title: Where the day's P&L came from
chapters.dek: A volatility book computes its P&L twice every day: once from prices, once from yesterday's risk. The first is the number. The second is whether you understand it.

figures.title: One day's P&L, by cause
figures.caption: Each bar starts where the last one ended. The first six add up to the change in the book's marked value; the last three are cash that never touched an option model.

checks.q: The stock was unchanged, implied vols were unchanged, and the book shows +$40,000 against a theta of −$5,000. No trades. What do you check first?
checks.right: The marks and the positions: something was re-marked, mis-booked, or hit by a corporate action
checks.why: Marks and positions. With no move in spot or vol, the greeks predict −$5,000 and the unexplained is $45,000. Intraday movement cannot produce it in a book that did not trade, and gamma earns nothing on a zero close-to-close move. An unexplained gain is the same problem as an unexplained loss, and it tends to reverse.

chapters.text: A small book on one stock at $100: long 200 ninety-day 100 calls, short 100 thirty-day 105 calls, and short 8,174 shares to make it delta-neutral at last night's close. Today the stock falls 2%, thirty-day vol rises a point and a half, ninety-day vol rises 0.8, and you buy 50 more calls three cents under your own mark. The figure builds the day's P&L one cause at a time. One day's P&L, by cause The day Each bar starts where the last one ended. The first six add up to the change in the book's marked value; the last three are cash that never touched an option model. The number itself is simple. Reprice every position at tonight's marks, subtract last night's value, and add the cash that moved. The book's marked value rose $1,752 . Carry added $64, the new trade $150, fees took $32, and the day is $1,934 . The explanation takes last night's greeks and today's moves and predicts that $1,752 without repricing anything: Delta, −$1. The book was hedged flat, so a 2% move earns nothing at first order. A large number here means the hedge was wrong or late. Gamma, +$192. Half the book's gamma times the move squared. This is the realized-volatility line: over a month, the sum of these against the sum of theta is whether the stock moved more than you paid for. Theta, −$274. One calendar day of decay, long options against short ones. On a Monday it is three days' worth. Vega, +$1,637. Each expiry's vega times that expiry's own vol change: the ninety-day calls made $3,135 and the short thirty-day calls lost $1,497. The book's summed vega is $2,920 a point, and a report that multiplied that by a single "vol up one point" would have said $2,920. Vega has to be attributed bucket by bucket or it explains nothing. Vanna and volga, +$212. The second-order terms: spot and vol moving together, and vol moving a long way. Small on a day like this, and the largest line on the days people remember. Unexplained, −$14. What is left when the predicted change is subtracted from the real one. Under one percent of the day here. [equation: P&L = Δ(marked value) + carry + new-trade edge − fees] Reads as: what the positions are worth tonight minus what they were worth last night, plus interest, borrow and dividends, plus the difference between where you traded and where you mark, less what you paid to trade. [equation: Δ(marked value) ≈ Δ·dS + ½Γ·dS² + Θ·dt + Σ vega_T·dσ_T + vanna·dS·dσ + ½ volga·dσ² + unexplained] Reads as: the move times delta, the move squared times half of gamma, the time passed times theta, each expiry's vol change times its vega, the cross terms, and whatever the list missed. Three lines sit outside the greeks, and on a real desk they are where the arguments are. Carry is interest on the cash the book holds or owes, the fee on borrowed shares, and dividends received or paid on stock positions. Here the short stock leaves the book holding about $703,000, which earns $87 a day at 4.5%, against $22 of borrow. It is small daily and large annually, and it is the line a conversion or reversal book lives on. New-trade edge is the gap between your fill and your own mark at the time. Buying 50 calls three cents under the mark books $150 today. It is real only if the mark is right, which is why desks watch whether positions bought "with edge" go on to make or lose money afterwards. The marks are not a line, but every line depends on them. Liquid options are marked near the mid; the rest are marked off a fitted surface, and moving that surface moves P&L with no trade at all. Vol funds therefore have the marks checked by someone who is not paid on them, against broker quotes or a pricing service. That is why the unexplained bar is the one a risk manager reads first. On an ordinary day it should be a few percent of the total. When it is not, the causes are a short list: a move big enough that third-order terms matter; a mark that changed for a reason other than the market; a trade booked wrong or missing; a dividend, split or other corporate action the model did not know about; or a position that is not what the system thinks it is. Four of those five are operations problems, found by reconciling positions and cash to the prime broker before anyone trusts the number. Above the desk the fund adds one more layer: trading P&L, less financing and expenses, gives the change in net asset value before management and performance fees. That part is accounting. The part worth being able to do in your head is the attribution. Try this A crash day: the stock falls 5%, thirty-day vol jumps six points and ninety-day three. Predict which bar grows most relative to the default day. Vanna and volga grow almost tenfold, from $212 to $2,044, and the unexplained goes from $14 to $214. On the quiet weekend there is only decay and carry: three days of theta cost $821 and three days of carry bring in $193.

chapters.title: The columns on the report, decoded
chapters.dek: Risk systems print a dozen fields with names like DollarGammaPct. Each is one of four greeks multiplied by something, and the something is where people go wrong.

figures.title: Every field for one position
figures.caption: Field names differ from one system to the next. The definitions in the last column are what to match against your own report, and the reprice figures are how to test it.

checks.q: A report shows DollarGammaPct of $200,000 on a hedged position. The stock moves 3%. Roughly what did gamma make?
checks.why: $9,000. Half of 200,000, times three squared, over a hundred. $6,000 multiplies by the move without squaring it; $18,000 forgets the half; $600,000 is the change in dollar delta, which is what you rehedge, not what you made.

chapters.text: One position: long 100 thirty-day 260 calls on a $250 stock at 30 vol. The table computes every field a typical report shows for it, from the definition, and where it can it checks the number by moving the input and repricing. Change the position and watch which fields scale with what. Every field for one position The position Field names differ from one system to the next. The definitions in the last column are what to match against your own report, and the reprice figures are how to test it. The three gamma fields are the ones that cause trouble, because they are the same quantity in three units. GammaShares, 173. Shares of delta the position gains when the stock rises $1. It answers "how many shares do I trade to rehedge a one-dollar move". DollarGamma, $43,316. Those 173 shares valued at $250. Dollars of delta gained per $1 move. DollarGammaPct, $108,289. Dollars of delta gained per 1% move. A 1% move here is $2.50, so the position gains 433 shares, worth $108,289. This is the version that compares across stocks, because a 1% move means the same thing on a $20 stock and a $500 one, and it is the "gamma cash" of chapter 01. The P&L that goes with it has a half in it. A hedged position that gains 433 shares over a $2.50 move was holding, on average, half of them along the way: half of 433 times $2.50 is $541 . [equation: DollarGammaPct = Γ × 100 × contracts × S² ÷ 100 P&L(x%) = ½ × DollarGammaPct × x² ÷ 100] Reads as: gamma in shares, times the stock price squared, per hundred; and a move of x percent pays half of that times x squared over a hundred. For a 2% move, multiply the 1% figure by four. The rest follow the same pattern: a per-share greek, times 100, times contracts, then into dollars. DollarDelta, $889,220, is the stock position that would move the same: 3,557 shares at $250. One percent of it, $8,892, is the P&L of a 1% move before gamma. Theta, −$1,439 a day, set against the $541 a 1% move pays, gives the break-even move of 1.63% : the daily move at which gamma earns back the decay. Vega, $2,670, is per volatility point. WeightedVega restates it for a move in one-month vol by scaling with the square root of 30 over the days to expiry, so a thirty-day option is unchanged and a one-year option counts for about 29% of its raw vega. Vanna, $14,157, is dollars of delta gained when vol rises a point, and Charm, −34 shares a day, is delta lost overnight with nothing moving. Both are deltas you did not trade, which is why they sit on a hedger's screen. Before trusting any of these on a system you did not build, pin down five conventions, because each has at least two versions in use: Per dollar or per percent. At a stock price of exactly $100, DollarGamma and DollarGammaPct are the same number, so a test on a $100 stock tells you nothing. At $250 they differ by 2.5 times. With or without the half. Some systems report the P&L of a 1% move and call it dollar gamma. That is $541 here, two hundred times smaller than $108,289. Per vol point or per unit of vol. Vega of $2,670 a point is $267,000 per 1.00 of volatility. Calendar or trading days. Theta per calendar day is about 31% smaller than theta per trading day, and only one of them is right for a Friday. Sign. Short positions should flip every field. A report that shows short options with positive gamma is showing the option's greek, not the position's. The test is always the same one the table runs: move the input by the stated amount, reprice, and see whether the field predicted the change. Try this Put the same option on a $100 stock with a 104 strike. Predict which two gamma fields become equal.

chapters.title: Check yourself
chapters.dek: Six questions across the page, and the series.

checks.q: Which of these adds cleanly across a book on one underlying?
checks.right: Dollar delta. Converting the rate into money first is what makes positions of different sizes comparable
checks.why: Dollar delta. Rates do not add across different position sizes; money does. This is the same units discipline that page 01's chapter 08 built the blotter around, applied to a whole book instead of one line.

checks.q: Roughly how wrong is a delta-plus-gamma estimate on a 20% move, for our book?
checks.right: About 58% — the book makes $36,971 and the estimate predicts $15,436
checks.why: About 58%. Error grows roughly with the cube of the move, so it is negligible at 1% and dominant at 20%. The practical consequence is that greeks are a hedging tool and the matrix is a limits tool, and swapping them is how books get sized wrongly.

checks.q: Our book's net vega is 417. What is the range of P&L across volatility moves that all average about two points?
checks.right: Roughly $743 to $1,238, because the book is long the front and back and short the belly. The net cannot distinguish a parallel move from a twist
checks.why: $743 to $1,238 — a spread of about 67%. The book is a term-structure position wearing the disguise of a modest long-vol book, and the disguise is the net vega number itself.

checks.q: Why does a scenario matrix use full repricing rather than greeks?
checks.right: Because the cells that matter are far from today's spot, which is exactly where a local expansion stops working. Full repricing does not degrade with distance
checks.why: Because the interesting cells are far away. The matrix is deliberately built where the approximation fails; using the approximation to build it would defeat the purpose. Full repricing costs more computation and the corners are the only place the extra cost buys anything.

checks.q: What is a limit breach actually telling you?
checks.right: That the position has grown past the size at which the firm is willing to find out. The correct response is to reduce rather than to argue about probability
checks.why: It is a statement about appetite, not a forecast. Limits are pre-committed answers to a question that becomes impossible to think about clearly once the scenario is actually happening — which is the entire reason they are set in advance.

checks.q: The book made $40,000 yesterday and the greeks predicted $5,000. What is the first thing to check?
checks.right: Your marks and your model. A large unexplained residual means the instrument producing every other number on the report is broken, and today's risk figures inherit that error
checks.why: Marks and model. An unexplained profit is exactly as alarming as an unexplained loss and considerably less likely to be investigated, which is precisely why it is worth naming as the first item in the routine. Attribution is a test of your instruments, and it happens to be denominated in money.
